text: 1.1. It is now time to demonstrate to the Greeks that the gnostic alone is truly devout, so that the philosophers, learning what kind of person the true Christian is, may condemn their own ignorance—since they persecute the name at random and without cause, and idly call atheists those who have come to know the God who truly is. With the philosophers it is fitting, I think, to use clearer arguments, drawn from their own learning, so that, already trained, they may be able to follow, even if they have not yet shown themselves worthy of partaking in the power to believe. For the present we shall not appeal to the words of the prophets; later, at the appropriate places, we shall make use of the Scriptures, but for now we shall indicate summarily what they reveal, sketching Christianity in outline, so that we may not break the continuity of the argument by introducing the Scriptures—and that to those who do not yet understand their language. But once we have shown what is meant, then the testimonies too will be made plain to them, when they believe out of abundance. (And even if what we say should appear to some of the multitude to differ from the Scriptures of the Lord, let it be known that it draws its breath and life from there, and that, taking its starting points from them, it professes to set forth their sense alone, not their wording.) For elaboration carried too far, if it is not made at the right moment, would reasonably seem superfluous; and to have given no thought at all to what is pressing is utterly slothful and deficient. But "blessed indeed are those who search out the testimonies of the Lord; with the whole heart will they seek him"; and the Law and the prophets bear witness concerning the Lord.

1.2. Our task, then, is to demonstrate that the gnostic alone is holy and devout, worshipping the true God in a manner worthy of God; and upon what is worthy of God there follow the being beloved of God and the love of God. He holds everything that excels to be honourable according to its worth: among objects of sense, rulers and parents and every elder are to be honoured; among objects of instruction, the most ancient philosophy and the most venerable prophecy; among objects of thought, that which is eldest in origin—the timeless and unoriginate Beginning and First-fruit of all that is, the Son. From him we may learn the cause beyond, the Father of all things, the most venerable and most beneficent of all, no longer handed down by speech, but to be revered by veneration and silence with holy awe—reverend and to be worshipped in the highest degree; spoken of, indeed, by the Lord as far as those who were learning could grasp, but apprehended only by those chosen out for knowledge by the Lord—"by those," as the Apostle says, "whose senses have been trained by exercise."

1.3. The service of God, then, for the gnostic is the unbroken care of his soul and his occupation with the divine through love that never ceases. For of the service rendered to men, one kind is that which improves, the other that which ministers. Medicine improves the body, philosophy the soul. From children to parents, and from subjects to rulers, there comes a ministering benefit. Likewise in the Church the presbyters preserve the image of that which improves, and the deacons that which ministers. Both these forms of service are rendered to God by the angels in the administration of earthly things, and by the gnostic himself, who ministers to God and displays to men the contemplation that improves, so that he may be appointed to teach for the correction of mankind. For he alone is devout who serves God well and irreproachably in human affairs. For just as the best tending of plants is that by which the fruits are produced and gathered through skill and agricultural experience, furnishing men with the benefit derived from them, so the devotion of the gnostic, taking up into itself the fruits of the men who through him have come to believe—as more and more are brought to recognition and so are saved—accomplishes through experience the best of harvests. And if godliness is a settled disposition preserving what is fitting toward God, then he alone who is godly is beloved of God; and this would be the man who knows what is fitting both in knowledge and in life, knowing how he ought to live who is to become, and is already being made, like to God.

1.4. In this way, then, he is first a lover of God. For as he who honours his father is a lover of his father, so he who honours God is a lover of God. And it appears to me that there are three results of the gnostic faculty: first, to know things; second, to perform whatever reason dictates; and third, to be able to hand on, in a manner worthy of God, the things hidden in the truth. He, then, who is persuaded that God is almighty and has learned the divine mysteries from his only-begotten Son—how is this man an atheist? For the atheist is he who does not believe that God exists; the superstitious man is he who fears the daemonic powers, who deifies everything—wood and stone and spirit—and enslaves the man who does not live according to reason.

2.5. Faith, then, in the knowledge of God is the first thing, together with the Saviour's teaching the conviction that to do wrong in no way whatever—this is what one must hold to be fitting to the knowledge of God. By this the most devout man is the most powerful being on earth, and the angel the most powerful in heaven, as being nearer in place and already partaking more purely of the eternal and blessed life. But most perfect and most holy and most sovereign and most ruling and most kingly and most beneficent is the nature of the Son, which is nearest to the one Almighty. This is the greatest pre-eminence, which orders all things according to the will of the Father and steers the whole most excellently, working all things with untiring and unwearied power, looking through the things by which it acts upon the hidden thoughts. For the Son of God never departs from his watch-tower, not being divided, not severed, not passing from place to place, but being everywhere always and contained nowhere—wholly mind, wholly the Father's light, wholly eye, seeing all things, hearing all things, knowing all things, searching the powers with power. To him is subject the whole host of angels and of gods—to the paternal Word who has taken up the holy administration "because of him who subjected" all to him, on whose account also are all his men: but some "by recognition," others not yet; and some as friends, others as faithful household servants, others simply as servants. This is the Teacher who trains the gnostic by mysteries.

2.6. He trains the believer by good hopes, and the hard of heart by corrective discipline through the action upon the senses. From this comes providence, in private and in public and everywhere. That there is a Son of God, and that he is the Saviour and Lord whom we proclaim, the divine prophecies plainly set forth. In this way the Lord of all, both Greeks and barbarians, persuades those who are willing; for he does not compel one who is able to receive salvation from him by choosing and by fulfilling all that comes from him toward laying hold of the hope. This is he who gives philosophy also to the Greeks through the inferior angels; for by ancient and divine command angels are distributed among the nations. But "the Lord's portion" is the glory of those who believe. For either the Lord does not care for all men—and this would come about either through inability, which is not permissible, for it is a sign of weakness, or through unwillingness while able, but the suffering is not the mark of a good being; nor is he slothful through luxury, who for our sakes took on suffering flesh—or else he cares for all alike, which indeed befits him who has become the Lord of all. For he is a Saviour, not of some and not of others; but to each in proportion to his fitness he distributes his benefit—to Greeks and barbarians, and to those among them who are foreordained and, in their own due season, called as faithful and elect.

2.7. He, then, who has called all alike, but has assigned special honours to those who have believed in a special way, would never envy any; nor would the Lord of all ever be hindered by another, especially since he ministers to the will of the good and almighty Father. But neither does envy touch the Lord, who came into being without beginning and is free from passion. Nor indeed are the affairs of men such as to be objects of the Lord's envy. The one who envies is another, one whom passion has touched. And it cannot be said that through ignorance the Lord is unwilling to save mankind, on the ground that he does not know how each is to be cared for. For ignorance does not touch the Son, who before the foundation of the world was the Father's counsellor. For this was the Wisdom "in which" the Almighty God "rejoiced"; for the Son is the "power of God," being the most sovereign Word of the Father before all things that have come to be, and rightly would he be called his "Wisdom" and the Teacher of those who were fashioned through him. Nor again, drawn aside by any pleasure, would he ever abandon the care of mankind, who indeed took up the flesh, which is by nature subject to passion, and trained it into the disposition of freedom from passion. And how could he be Saviour and Lord, if he were not Saviour and Lord of all? Rather, he is Saviour of those who have believed, because they have willed to know, and Lord of the disobedient, until, being able to confess, they obtain through him a benefit suited and proportioned to them. And every activity of the Lord has its reference to the Almighty, and the Son is, so to speak, a kind of paternal energy.

2.8. The Saviour, then, could never be a hater of men, who through his surpassing love of mankind did not disdain the weakness of human flesh, but put it on and came for the common salvation of men; for the faith of those who choose it is common. Nor would he ever neglect his own work, since to man alone of all living creatures the conception of God was instilled at his creation. Nor could there be for God any better or more harmonious ordering of mankind than the one appointed. For it is always fitting that the better should by nature rule the worse, and that to the one able to administer something well should be assigned the management of that other. And the true ruler and governor is the divine Word and his providence, which surveys all things and overlooks the care of none of its own. These would be those who have chosen to be his own—those who through faith are being perfected. Thus the Son is established, by the will of the almighty Father, as the cause of all good things, the first author of motion, a power not to be grasped by sense. For he was not seen as what he was by those unable to receive him because of the weakness of the flesh; rather, taking on flesh perceptible to sense, he came to show what is possible for men through obedience to the commandments. Being therefore the paternal power, he easily prevails over whatever he wills.

2.9. He leaves not the least part of his administration uncared for; otherwise the whole would no longer have been well wrought by him. But it is, I think, the mark of the greatest power that the examination of all the parts, even to the smallest, should proceed with exactness—all things looking toward the first Governor of the universe, who by the Father's will steers the salvation of all, while others are appointed under others as rulers, until one comes at last to the great High Priest. For from one Beginning above, which works according to the will, depend the first and second and third orders; then at the summit of the visible world is the blessed company of angels; and so on down even to us, some set under others, out of one and through one being saved and saving, are they ordered in their ranks. As, then, even a far-distant piece of iron is moved together by the breath of the Heraclean stone, drawn out through many iron rings, so too those drawn by the Holy Spirit—the virtuous are made akin to the first abode, and the rest in turn down to the last—while those who are evil through weakness, having fallen into a bad condition through unjust greed, neither holding nor being held, are swept away, entangled by the passions, and fall to the ground. For this is the law from above: that whoever wills should choose virtue.

2.10. Therefore the commandments, both those under the Law and those before the Law—not laid down for the lawful (for "the law is not laid down for the just")—appointed that the one who chooses life should receive eternal life and a blessed reward; and that the one, again, who delights in evil should be granted to dwell with those he has chosen; and again, that the soul which is at every point being improved into the recognition of virtue and the increase of righteousness should receive a better rank in the universe, "stretching forward" at each advance toward the disposition of freedom from passion, until it "arrives at the perfect man," the pre-eminence of knowledge and of inheritance together. These saving revolutions are apportioned according to the order of the change, by times and places and honours and kinds of knowledge and inheritances and ministries—each according to each—up to the higher and immediate contemplation of the Lord in eternity. For what is lovely draws toward the contemplation of itself everyone who has wholly set himself, by the love of knowledge, upon contemplation.

2.11. Therefore the Lord too, drawing from one fountain the commandments which he gave, both the earlier and the later, neither overlooked those before the Law as lawless, nor again permitted those who did not heed the barbarian philosophy to break free unbridled. For giving commandments to the one and philosophy to the other, he "shut up" unbelief until the coming; whence everyone who has not believed is without excuse. For from either kind of advance, the Greek and the barbarian, he leads on to the perfection that is through faith. And if any of the Greeks, passing over the preliminary stage of Greek philosophy, has set out at once for the true teaching, this man, even though unschooled, has outrun the rest, having chosen the short road to salvation through faith unto perfection.

2.12. Everything, then, that did not hinder a man's choice from being voluntary, God both made and showed to be helpful toward virtue, so that in some way, even to those who can discern but dimly, the one truly almighty God might be shown to be good, saving from age to age through the Son, but in no way and by no means the cause of evil. For toward the salvation of the whole all things have been ordered by the Lord of the universe, both in general and in particular. It is therefore the work of saving righteousness ever to lead each forward to the better, as far as may be. For with a view to the salvation and continuance of the higher, even the lesser things are administered in proportion to their characters. Thus all that is virtuous passes over into better dwellings, having for the cause of its change the choice of knowledge, which the soul held as its own sovereign possession. But the necessary chastisements, through the goodness of the great Judge who watches over all, both through the angels who are near and through varied prior judgements and through the final judgement, compel to repentance those who have grown more "callous."

3.13. "But concerning the rest I am silent," glorifying the Lord. Yet of those gnostic souls I do speak—souls which by the magnificence of their contemplation surpass the polity of each holy order, in accordance with which the blessed dwellings of the gods are distinguished and allotted; souls counted holy among the holy, transferred whole out of whole, arriving at better places out of better, no longer embracing the divine contemplation in mirrors or through mirrors, but feasting, as much as may be, on the vision clear and most exactly pure—a vision insatiable to souls that love it with a more than natural love—reaping eternally an eternal gladness, all honoured to remain in the sameness of pre-eminence. This is the comprehending contemplation of "the pure in heart." This, then, is the activity of the perfected gnostic: to hold communion with God through the great High Priest, being made like to the Lord, so far as may be, through all his service toward God—a service that reaches out to the salvation of men by care for the benefit done to us, and again by ministry, by teaching, and by well-doing in deeds. Yes, the gnostic both founds and fashions himself, and besides adorns those who give heed to him, being made like to God, by likening to freedom from passion—so far as may be—the freedom from passion gathered through discipline to that which possesses it by nature; and this while holding communion and dwelling with the Lord "without distraction." Gentleness, I think, and love of mankind and magnificent godliness are the standards of gnostic assimilation.

3.14. These virtues, I say, are "an acceptable sacrifice" with God—the unproud heart with right knowledge, which Scripture calls "a whole burnt offering to God," when the whole man who has been taken up into holiness is enlightened into undivided union. For both the Gospel and the Apostle command us to take ourselves captive and to slay our own selves—putting to death "the old man, corrupted according to its desires," and raising up "the new man" from the death of the old perversion—laying aside the passions and becoming free from sin. This, then, was what the Law too hinted at when it commanded the sinner to be put to death: the passing over from death to life, the freedom from passion that comes of faith. Not understanding this, the teachers of the Law, taking it as a thing for contention, have furnished occasions to those who try in vain to slander it. For this reason we reasonably do not sacrifice to God, who is in need of nothing, who has furnished all things to all; but the one who was offered up for us we glorify by offering up ourselves—from that which is needless of nothing into needing nothing, and from that which is free of passion into freedom from passion. For God rejoices in our salvation alone. Reasonably, then, to him who is not conquered by pleasures we offer no sacrifice down here—not even as high as the densest clouds, but far short even of these, while the steam of smoke reaches only as far as it reaches.

3.15. The Divine, then, is neither in need, nor a lover of pleasure, nor a lover of gain or of money; being full, and furnishing all things to every created and needy thing, it is not charmed by sacrifices nor by votive offerings nor by glory and honour, nor is it led aside by any such things. Rather it shows itself like good and noble men, who would never betray the just—whether through fear of a threatened danger or by the promise of greater gifts. But as many as have not perceived the self-determined and unenslaved character of the human soul as regards its choice of life, being vexed at the things done through the injustice that comes of want of education, do not believe that God exists. Of the same opinion are those who, falling into the incontinence of pleasures and into excessive griefs and unwilled misfortunes, and giving way under their calamities, say that there is no God, or that, if he exists, he does not oversee all things. Others again are persuaded that those reckoned as gods can be won over by sacrifices and gifts, lending their aid, so to speak, to the men's own excesses; and these are not even willing to believe that the only true God exists—he who abides in the sameness of just goodness.

3.16. The gnostic, then, is devout—he who cares first for himself, and then for his neighbours, that we may become as good as possible. For the son too gives delight to a good father by showing himself diligent and like his father, and the subject to the ruler; for to believe and to obey lies in our power. The cause of evils one might take to be the weakness of matter and the unwilled impulses of ignorance and the irrational necessities that come of want of learning. The gnostic, having through learning risen above these as above wild beasts, and imitating the divine purpose, does good to those of mankind who are willing, so far as he can. And if ever he comes into a position of rule, like Moses, he will govern for the salvation of the governed, and will tame what is wild and unpersuaded, honouring the best and chastising the wicked—chastisement being inscribed, in accordance with reason, for instruction. For above all things the soul of a just man is a divine image and like to God, in which, through obedience to the precepts, there is enshrined and set up the Ruler of all things mortal and immortal, the King and Begetter of all that is noble—who is in truth law and ordinance and eternal Reason, being one Saviour both to each privately and to all in common. This is he who is truly only-begotten, the express character of the glory of the all-ruling and almighty Father, who stamps upon the gnostic the perfect contemplation according to his own image—so that there is now a third divine image, made like, as far as may be, to the second cause, to the true Life, through which we live the true life—copying out, as it were, the gnostic stamp that has become ours, conversant with things firm and wholly unchanging.

3.17. Ruling, then, over himself and his own, possessing a firm grasp of the divine knowledge, he comes near to the truth in genuine fashion. For the knowledge and firm grasp of things intelligible may rightly be called science; its work concerning things divine is to consider what the first cause is, and what it is "through which all things were made and without which nothing has come to be"; and again, what things are, as it were, pervading, and what containing; what are conjoined, and what disjoined; and what rank each of these holds, and what power and what office each contributes. And again, among human things, to consider what man himself is, and what is for him according to nature or contrary to nature; how he ought to act or to be acted upon; what his virtues are, and what his vices; and the questions of goods and evils and things intermediate, and all that concerns courage and prudence and temperance, and that perfect virtue which crowns them all, righteousness. But prudence and righteousness he uses toward the acquisition of wisdom; and courage not only in enduring adverse circumstances, but in mastering pleasure and desire, grief and anger as well, and, in general, in setting himself against everything that allures us, whether by violence or by some deceit. For one must not endure vices and evils, but thrust them away; and one must endure things fearful. Useful, therefore, even pain is found to be, in medicine and in teaching and in chastisement; and through it characters are set right for the benefit of mankind.

3.18. The forms of courage are steadfastness, greatness of mind, magnanimity, liberality, and magnificence. For this reason the gnostic is touched neither by the blame nor by the ill repute that comes from the many, nor is he subject to opinions or to flatteries; and in enduring toils, while at the same time accomplishing something of what befits him, and rising courageously above all circumstances, he shows himself a true man among the rest of men. And again, preserving prudence, he is temperate in the quietness of his soul, receptive of the noble things that are promised as his own, in the turning away from base things as alien—becoming orderly and above the world, doing all things in order and arrangement and erring in nothing anywhere; rich, indeed, in the highest degree, by desiring nothing, since he has few needs and is in the abundance of every good through the knowledge of the Good. For the first work of his righteousness is to pass his life in love with his own kind, and to dwell with them both on earth and in heaven.

3.19. In this way he is also liberal in giving, when he has the means, and a lover of mankind, being the bitterest hater of wickedness through his perfect turning away from all evil-doing. He must learn, then, to be faithful both to himself and to his neighbours and obedient to the commandments. For this is "the servant of God"—he who is willingly led by the commandments. But he who now, not for the commandments' sake but for the sake of knowledge itself, is "pure in heart"—this man is "the friend of God." For neither are we born possessing virtue by nature, nor does it come to us by nature afterwards, once we are born, as do certain other parts of the body (since then it would no longer be voluntary or praiseworthy); nor again is virtue perfected, as language is, out of the things that befall us and the habit thereby formed (for it is in nearly this way that vice arises). Nor does knowledge come about from any art, whether of those that provide a livelihood or of those that tend the body; nor yet from the ordinary cycle of education—it is enough if these can but prepare and serve the soul. For the political laws can perhaps restrain wicked acts;

3.20. but neither they themselves, nor persuasive arguments, being superficial, could provide a scientific and abiding hold upon the truth. Greek philosophy, as it were, purifies the soul beforehand and prepares it for the reception of faith, upon which the truth builds up knowledge. This is he—this is the true athlete in the great stadium, the fair world, who is crowned with the true victory over all the passions. For the president of the games is the almighty God, the umpire is the only-begotten Son of God, and the spectators are angels and gods; and the all-contending struggle is "not against blood and flesh," but against the "spiritual powers" of inordinate passions that work through fleshly things. Prevailing over these great adversaries, and having contended as in certain contests against the tempter who hangs over him, he wins the prize of immortality. For the verdict of God toward the most just judgement cannot be deceived. The theatre, then, is summoned to the contest, and the athletes contend in the stadium; and out of these he prevails who has become obedient to his trainer. For all things lie equally before all from God, and he himself is blameless; but the one who is able will choose, and the one who has willed will prevail. For this reason too we have received mind, that we may know what we do; and the "Know thyself" means, here, to know to what end we have come to be. And we have come to be in order to be obedient to the commandments, if we choose to will our own salvation. This, perhaps, is Adrasteia—the inevitable—by which there is no escaping God.

3.21. The human work, then, is ready obedience to God, who has proclaimed a manifold salvation through commandments; and well-pleasing is acknowledgement. For the benefactor takes the first step in well-doing, and he who receives it readily, with the due reflections, and keeps the commandments, this man is faithful; and he who, as far as he is able, requites the well-doing with the well-doing of love, is now a friend. There is one chief requital on the part of men: to do those things that are pleasing to God. And just as the Teacher and Saviour receives the benefits done to men, and their correction, as though they were his own offspring and a kind of kindred result, reckoning them to his own favour and honour—just as he reckons the injuries done to those who have believed in him as his own ungratefulness and dishonour (for what other dishonour could touch God?)—so it is that there is no other requital worthy of so great a salvation that one could render in return for the benefit from the Lord. But as those who do harm to property insult the masters, and as those who harm soldiers harm their commander, so the maltreatment of those consecrated to the Lord is disregard of the Lord himself. For just as the sun illuminates not only heaven and the whole world, lighting up earth and sea, but also through windows and a small chink sends its ray into the innermost chambers, so the Word, poured out everywhere, looks upon even the smallest acts of life.

4.22. But the Greeks suppose their gods to be, like men, both in form and in passion; and as each people paint their forms like to themselves—as Xenophanes says, "the Ethiopians black and snub-nosed, the Thracians red-haired and grey-eyed"—so too they fashion the souls of their gods like to their own. The barbarians, accordingly, make them beastlike and savage in character, and the Greeks gentler, yet still subject to passion. For this reason it is reasonable that the wicked should have base conceptions about God, and the good the best; and on this account he who is truly "kingly in soul," and is gnostic and devout and free from superstition, is persuaded that the only God is honourable, august, magnificent, well-doing, beneficent, the author of all good things, but in no way the cause of evils. And concerning Greek superstition we have, I think, set things forth sufficiently in our treatise entitled the Exhortation, making free use of the relevant history as need pressed. There is no call, then, "to tell over again as a tale what has been clearly said."

4.23. Yet, as far as to take note of it while we are upon the subject, a few points out of many will suffice—and these alone serve to show that those who liken the Divine to the worst of men are atheists. For either the gods are harmed by men, and are shown by us to be worse than men in being harmed by them; or, if not this, then how is it that, in cases where they are not harmed, they grow bitter—like some irascible old woman provoked to anger—as men say that Artemis was wroth with the Aetolians on account of Oeneus? For how did she not reason, being a goddess, that Oeneus had not despised her, but had either forgotten, or had neglected the matter as though he had already sacrificed? Well too does Auge plead her cause against Athena for being angry with her because she had given birth in the temple, saying: "You rejoice to look on the spoils that destroy mortals, and the wreckage of the dead, and these are not defilement to you; but if I have given birth, you count this a dreadful thing." And yet the other animals too, giving birth in the temples, do no wrong.

4.24. Reasonably, then, the superstitious, becoming credulous about those easily moved to anger, take all that befalls them to be signs and causes of evils. If a mouse should dig through an altar that is made of clay, or, having nothing else, should gnaw through a bag; if a fowl that is being reared should crow at evening—they set this down as a sign of something. Menander mocks just such a man in his Superstitious Man: "May some good thing befall me, O most honoured gods! For as I was putting on my shoe I broke the strap of my right sandal." "Reasonably, you babbler; for it was rotten, and you, being mean, would not buy a new pair." Charming is the saying of Antiphon. When a man took it for an omen that a sow had eaten her piglets, Antiphon, seeing that she had been wasted by hunger through the meanness of the one who fed her, said: "Rejoice at the omen, that, being so hungry, she did not eat your children." "And what is there to wonder at," says Bion, "if the mouse gnawed through the bag, finding nothing to eat? For it would have been a wonder if—as Arcesilaus jestingly suggested—the bag had eaten the mouse."

4.25. Well too did Diogenes say to the man who marvelled that he had found the serpent coiled about the pestle: "Do not marvel; for that would have been the stranger thing, had you seen the pestle coiled about the upright serpent." For the irrational animals too must run and dart, fight, bring forth, and die—things which, being according to nature for them, could never be contrary to nature for us. "And many birds beneath the sun's rays go to and fro." The comic poet Philemon too mocks such things: "Whenever I see," he says, "a man watching closely who sneezed or who spoke, or who it is that goes before him, scanning it all—I sell that man at once in the market-place. Each of us walks for himself, and speaks and sneezes; things come to pass for us in the city according to their nature." Then, sober, men ask for health; but, gorging themselves and rolling in drunkenness at the festivals, they draw diseases upon themselves.

4.26. Many fear also the inscriptions that are set up. Very neatly did Diogenes, finding written over the house of a worthless man, "The glorious victor Heracles dwells here; let no evil enter in," say: "And how then shall the master of the house come in?" These same men, worshipping every piece of wood and every stone, as the saying goes—anointing them—stand in dread of red wool and lumps of salt and torches, of squill and brimstone, being bewitched by the sorcerers with their unclean purifications. But God—the God who truly is—knows only the character of the just as holy, just as that of the unjust and wicked is accursed. One may indeed see that the eggs of birds that have undergone such purifications, if warmed, are still quickened into life; and this would not happen if they had taken up the evils of the one purified. Charmingly too the comic poet Diphilus mocks the sorcerers in these lines: "Purifying the daughters of Proetus, and their father Proetus son of Abas, and a fifth, an old crone besides—with one torch and one squill, for so many bodies of men—with brimstone and bitumen and the loud-roaring sea, from gently-flowing, deep-flowing Ocean. But, blessed Air, send through the clouds for hellebore, that I may make this bug into a drone."

4.27. Well too says Menander: "If you had some real evil, Phidias, you would need to seek a real remedy for it; but as it is, you have none. Find then an empty remedy for the empty trouble, and think that something does you good. Let the women wipe you all round in a circle and burn incense about you; sprinkle yourself with water from three springs, having thrown in salt and lentils." Pure is everyone who is conscious of no evil in himself. Tragedy, accordingly, says: "Orestes, what disease destroys you?" "The consciousness—that I know I have done dreadful things." For in truth purity is nothing else than abstinence from sins. Well, then, does Epicharmus say: "If you keep your mind pure, you are pure in your whole body." So too we say that one must first purify the souls from base and wicked doctrines through right reason, and then, in that way, turn to the recollection of the chief points set forth before. For even before the delivery of the mysteries they think it right to bring certain purifications to those who are about to be initiated, since one must lay aside the godless opinion and turn to the true tradition.

5.28. For is it not nobly and truly that we neither circumscribe in a place the Uncontainable, nor shut up in shrines "made with hands" that which contains all things? What holy work could belong to builders and stone-cutters and the mechanic's craft? Are not those better than these who have judged the air and the encompassing—nay rather the whole world and the universe—worthy of the pre-eminence of God? It would indeed be ridiculous, as the philosophers themselves say, that man, being "the plaything of God," should fashion God, and that God should become a game of art. For the thing produced is the same as, and like to, that out of which it is produced: the ivory thing is of ivory, and the golden of gold. But the statues and shrines wrought by mechanic men come into being out of inert matter, so that they too would be inert and material and profane; and even if you perfect the art, it has shared in the mechanic's labour. No longer, then, are the works of the art holy and divine. And what could be set up at all, when nothing is unestablished, since all things are in a place? But the thing established by another is established as having previously been unestablished. If, then, God is established by men, he was once unestablished, and so did not exist at all.

5.29. For that would be unestablished which is not—since everything that is not is established; but that which is could not be established by that which is not, nor indeed by another that is, for it too is. It remains, then, that it should be established by itself. But how shall a thing beget itself? Or how shall Being itself establish itself in being? Did it, being previously unestablished, then establish itself? But it would not even have existed, since that which is not is unestablished; and how should that which is reckoned to have been established—having already possessed being—afterwards make itself? And that of which all beings are—how should this stand in need of anything? But if the Divine were of human form, it would need the same things as man: food and shelter, a house and all that follows. For those of like shape and like passions will need a like manner of life. And if the sacred is understood in two ways—both God himself and the structure raised for his honour—how shall we not most properly call the Church, which has become holy unto the honour of God by recognition of him, a temple of God, the thing of great worth and not built by the mechanic's craft, nor decked out by a charlatan's hand, but made into a shrine by the will of God? For it is not the place but the assembly of the elect that I call the Church. This is the better temple for the reception of the greatness of God's worth. For the living being of great worth is consecrated, through surpassing holiness, to him who is worth the whole, or rather worth more than all things. And this man would be the gnostic, of great worth and precious to God, in whom God is established—that is, the knowledge of God is consecrated. Here too we should find the image, the divine and holy statue, in the just soul, when it is itself blessed, as having been purified beforehand, and blessed in performing blessed deeds. Here too is both that which is established and that which is being established: the one in those already gnostic, the other in those capable of becoming so, even if they are not yet worthy to receive the knowledge of God. For everyone who is going to believe is already faithful to God, and is consecrated, a virtuous statue set up unto honour, dedicated to God.

6.30. As, then, God is not circumscribed in a place, nor ever imaged in the shape of a living creature, so neither is he subject to passion nor in need, as created things are—as to desire sacrifices, in the manner of food, through hunger. Things that passion touches are all corruptible; and to offer food to one who needs no nourishment is vain. And that comic poet Pherecrates, in his Deserters, has charmingly represented the gods themselves blaming men over their sacrifices: "When you sacrifice to the gods, first of all you set apart for the priests their customary portion, and then for yourselves; and then—shame to tell it—having stripped the two thighs clean to the groin, you devour all the flesh and the loin clean bare, and the rest—the very vertebra—you scour as with a file, and then portion it out to us as if to dogs; and then, ashamed before one another, you hide it under heaps of barley-cakes." And Eubulus, himself also a comic poet, writes thus somewhere about sacrifices: "To the gods themselves you sacrifice only the tail and the thigh, as though to pederasts." And bringing on Dionysus in his Semele, he has made him expostulate: "First of all, whenever any sacrifice to me, they sacrifice blood, the bladder, the liver, the heart, and the surface membrane; for I myself eat neither sweetmeats nor thigh-pieces."

6.31. Menander too has represented the loins' end and the gall: "Laying upon the gods the inedible bones," he says, "they themselves consume the rest." Or is not the steam of whole burnt offerings to be shunned even by wild beasts? And if the steam is in truth a privilege of the gods of the Greeks, they would do well to deify their cooks as well, who are reckoned worthy of the same happiness, and to worship the very oven, which comes nearer to the much-prized steam. And Hesiod somewhere, regarding a division of meats by which Zeus was deceived by Prometheus, says that Zeus took "the white bones of an ox, by a cunning art" covered "with white fat"; and that thereafter "the tribes of men upon earth burn white bones to the immortals upon the fragrant altars." But they say that in no way is God nourished by being harmed through a desire arising from want. So then they will make him like a plant, nourished without appetite, and like beasts that lie hidden in their lairs. For they say these creatures grow harmlessly, fed either by the thickness of the surrounding air or by the very exhalation of their own bodies. And yet, if the Divine is nourished by them without need, what further need has the needless of nourishment? But if, being by nature in need of nothing, he rejoices in being honoured, then not unreasonably do we honour God through prayer, and send up this best and holiest sacrifice with righteousness, doing homage by the most righteous Word, through whom we receive knowledge, and through him glorifying the one we have learned. There is, then, among us this altar here below, the earthly one—the assembly of those who are dedicated to prayers, having, as it were, one common voice and one mind. And nourishments through the sense of smell, even if they are more divine than those through the mouth, are still signs of breathing. What, then, do they say about God?

6.32. Does he breathe out and in, like the race of daemons? Or does he only breathe in, like creatures of the water by the opening of their gills? Or does he breathe round about, like insects by the contraction of the body through the pressure of the wings? But they would liken God to none of these, if they were of sound mind. For all things that breathe draw in the air by the contraction of the lungs against the chest. Then, if they were to assign to God entrails and arteries and veins and nerves and members, they will be introducing him as in no way differing from these. But the breathing-together is rightly spoken of in regard to the Church. For the sacrifice of the Church is the word sent up as a fragrant offering from holy souls, while at the same time, together with the sacrifice, the whole mind is laid open to God. But they say that the most ancient altar in Delos was held to be pure, and that to it alone Pythagoras drew near, not defiled by slaughter and death—and will they disbelieve us when we call the just soul the truly holy altar, and the holy prayer that rises from it the incense? But sacrifices, I think, were devised by men under pretext of eating flesh; for it was possible, even otherwise, without such idolatry, for whoever wished to partake of meats. For the sacrifices according to the Law allegorize our piety, just as the turtle-dove and the pigeon offered for sins indicate to God the acceptable purification of the irrational part of the soul. But if any of the just does not burden his soul with the eating of meats, he uses a reasonable principle—not the one with which Pythagoras and his followers dream of the transmigration of the soul. Xenocrates, treating the subject specially in his work On Nourishment from Animals, and Polemon in his treatises On Life according to Nature, seem clearly to say that nourishment through flesh is unprofitable, since, being already worked over, it assimilates to the souls of the irrational creatures.

6.33. For this reason, indeed, the Jews especially abstain from swine's flesh, as though this beast were unclean, since beyond the rest it roots up and destroys the crops. But if they say that the animals are given to men, we too agree—only not by all means for food, nor indeed all of them, but those that are useless for work. Therefore not amiss does the comic poet Plato say in his play The Feasts: "Of four-footed beasts we ought henceforth to kill none but swine; for their flesh is most pleasant, and nothing comes from the pig but bristles and mud and squealing for us." Whence too Aesop said, not amiss, that swine squeal loudest when they are dragged off, knowing in themselves that they are good for nothing else but sacrifice. For which reason Cleanthes too says that they have soul instead of salt, that their flesh may not rot. Some, then, eat them as useless; others abstain as from a thing destructive of the crops; and others do not eat them because the creature is prone to coupling. In this way too the Law does not sacrifice the goat, except in the single rite of the sending-away of evils, since pleasure is the metropolis of vice. And indeed they say that the eating of goat's flesh contributes to epilepsy. They say also that the greatest distribution arises from swine's flesh, and therefore it is useful to those who train the body, but no longer to those who labour to increase the soul itself, on account of the sluggishness that comes from flesh-eating.

6.34. And now: land animals and birds, breathing the same air as our souls, are nourished by it, having a soul akin to the air; but they say that fishes do not breathe this air, but that other one which was mingled with the water straightway at the first creation, as it was with the rest of the elements—which is also a token of their material permanence. One must, then, "offer to God sacrifices that are not costly, but dear to God." And that compound incense in the Law, made up of many tongues and voices in prayer—or rather that which is prepared out of diverse nations and natures by the gift of the covenants "into the unity of faith," and gathered together in praises, with a pure mind, with a just and upright polity, out of holy works and righteous prayer. For who is so foolish, in the words of the poet's grace, and so utterly slack and credulous of men, as to hope that the gods take delight in bones without flesh and in burning gall—things not even edible to hungry dogs—and that all of them obtain this as a privilege, and pay back a return of thanks to those who do it, even if they happen to be pirates or robbers or tyrants? But we say that the fire sanctifies not the flesh, but sinful souls—meaning by fire not that which devours all and is mechanic, but the prudent fire, that which "pierces through the soul" that passes through the fire.

7.35. We are commanded to reverence and honour the Word, being persuaded that he is Saviour and Ruler, and through him the Father—not on chosen days, as some others do, but doing this continually through the whole of life and in every way. Indeed "the elect race," it is said, "Seven times in the day have I praised you," being justified according to the commandment. Whence the gnostic honours God neither in a fixed place, nor in a chosen shrine, nor on certain festivals and appointed days, but through his whole life, in every place—whether he happens to be alone by himself, or has with him some who have believed as he has: that is, he gives thanks for his knowledge and for his manner of life. And if the presence of one good man, through the shame and reverence it inspires, ever shapes the one who meets him toward the better, how shall not the man who is ever present, through knowledge and life and thanksgiving, with God unceasingly, with good reason be at every point better than himself in all things—in his deeds, his words, and his disposition? Such is he who is persuaded that God is present everywhere, and does not suppose him shut up in certain fixed places, so that, thinking himself sometimes apart from God, he might indulge in licence by night and by day. Keeping festival, then, through the whole of life, persuaded that God is present everywhere and on every side, we till the ground praising him, we sail singing hymns, and in the rest of our conduct we move skilfully. The gnostic comes nearer to being made the household of God, being grave and at the same time cheerful in all things—grave on account of his turning toward the Divine, cheerful on account of his reckoning up of the human goods which God has given us. The prophet sets forth the excellence of knowledge in this way:

7.36. "Goodness and discipline and knowledge teach me"—exalting the leading faculty of perfection by a gradual ascent. This man, then, is in truth the kingly man; this is the holy priest of God. Which thing even now is preserved among the most learned of the barbarians, who advance the priestly race to kingship. This man, then, in no way gives himself over to the rabble-rout that lords it in the theatres; the things said and done and seen there for the sake of dissolute pleasure he does not admit even in a dream—neither these pleasures of the spectacle nor the varied delights of the rest of the enjoyments: the costliness of incense that bewitches the sense of smell, the contrivings of dishes, the relishings of various wines that entice the taste, nor the many-flowered and fragrant garlands that effeminate the soul through the senses. But referring the august enjoyment of all things ever to God, of his food and his drink and his anointing he offers first-fruits to the Giver of all, acknowledging the favour both of the gift and of its use, through the Word given to him. He rarely comes to banquets and drinking-parties, except when the prospect of friendship and concord that the gathering holds out should urge him to go. For he is persuaded that God knows and hears all things—not only the voice, but the very thought; since hearing in us, though it works through bodily passages, receives its apprehension not through bodily power, but through a certain perception of the soul, and through the understanding that discriminates the voices which signify anything.

7.37. God, then, is not of human form, for this end—that he may hear; nor does he need senses, as the Stoics held, especially hearing and sight, on the ground that he could not otherwise apprehend. Rather, both the responsiveness of the air and the keenest joint-perception of the angels, and the power of the conscience that touches the soul, by a certain unspeakable power and apart from hearing through the senses, knows all things together with the thought. And even if one should say that the voice does not reach to God, but rolls below about the air, yet the thoughts of the saints cut through not only the air, but the whole world. And the divine power, like light, reaches through to discern the whole soul. What then? Do not the purposes also reach to God, sending forth their own voice? And are they not borne onward by the conscience? And for what voice would he wait who knows beforehand, according to his purpose, the elect one even before his birth, and what will be as though it already were? Or does not the light of his power shine everywhere into the depth of the whole soul, "searching the storehouses," as Scripture says, "with the lamp" of his power? For God is wholly hearing and wholly eye—if one may use these names.

7.38. In general, then, the conception of God that is unfitting, whether in hymns or in words, or even in writings or in doctrines—but which turns aside into low and unseemly notions and suppositions—preserves no godliness at all. Whence the praise of the many differs in no way from blasphemy, through ignorance of the truth. The prayers of men are of the same things as their appetites and desires and, in a word, their impulses. For this reason no one desires drink, but the drinking of the draught; nor an inheritance, but to inherit; and just so, not knowledge, but to know; nor even right citizenship, but to live as a citizen. The prayers, then, are of those things of which there are also requests, and the requests of those things of which there are also desires; and to pray and to reach out is done correspondingly toward having the goods and the benefits that accompany the possession. Always, then, the gnostic makes his prayer and request for the truly good things, those that concern the soul, and prays, working at the same time himself as well, to come into a settled disposition of goodness—so as no longer to have the good things laid up beside him, like certain lessons learned, but to be good.

7.39. Therefore it befits especially these men to pray—those who both know the Divine as they ought and have the virtue suited to him, who know what the truly good things are, and what one ought to ask, and when, and how, in each case. But it is the height of ignorance to ask things of those who are not gods as though they were gods, or to ask things that do not profit, asking evils for oneself under an appearance of goods. Whence, reasonably, since the good God is one, we pray—both we and the angels—that from him alone some of the good things may be given and others may abide. Yet not in like manner. For it is not the same thing to ask that a gift may abide, and to be eager to receive the beginning of it. And the turning away of evils is a kind of prayer. But this kind of prayer must never be used toward the harm of men—unless the gnostic, contriving the turning of the unjust toward righteousness, should so frame his request for those who have grown "callous." Prayer, then, is, to speak somewhat boldly, converse with God. And even if, whispering, not so much as opening our lips, we speak in silence, yet within we cry aloud; for God unceasingly hears all the inward converse.

7.40. For this reason too we lift up the head and raise the hands to heaven, and rise upon the feet at the closing utterance of the prayer, following the eagerness of the spirit toward the intelligible essence; and, striving to lift the body from the earth together with the word, we make "the soul winged" by longing for the better things, and force our way toward "the holy places," counting as nothing the bond of the flesh. For we know well that the gnostic makes voluntarily his going-out from the whole world—just as the Jews did from Egypt—showing plainly, more than by anything else, that he will be as near as possible to God. And if some assign also fixed hours to prayer—as the third, say, and the sixth and the ninth—yet the gnostic prays throughout his whole life, striving through prayer to be with God, and to leave behind, to speak briefly, all that is of no use to him once he has come to be there: as one who has already received here below the perfection of the conduct that springs from love. And the divisions of the hours into three, honoured with equal prayers, are known also to those who recognize the blessed Triad of the holy abodes.

7.41. Having come to this point, I was reminded of the doctrines introduced by certain heterodox men concerning the supposed needlessness of prayer—that is, by those of the school of Prodicus. Lest, then, they should be puffed up over this godless cleverness of theirs as though it were a strange new sect, let them learn that it was anticipated by the philosophers called Cyrenaics. Nevertheless this unholy knowledge of theirs, falsely so named, shall meet with refutation at the proper time, so that it may not now, slipping into these notes—being no small thing, this onslaught of theirs—break the continuity of the argument in hand, while we are showing that he alone is truly holy and devout who is in truth gnostic according to the rule of the Church, to whom alone the request is assigned according to the will of God, both when he asks and when he merely thinks it. For as God is able to do all that he wills, so the gnostic "receives all that he asks." For God knows in general both those who are worthy of good things and those who are not; whence he gives to each what befits them. Therefore he would often not give to the unworthy who ask, but would give to those who are plainly worthy. Yet the request is not idle, even if the good things are given apart from the asking. So then both thanksgiving and the request for the conversion of one's neighbours is the work of the gnostic. In this way the Lord too prayed, giving thanks for the things in which he completed his ministry, and praying that as many as possible might come to recognition, that among those being saved, through the salvation that comes of recognition, God might be glorified, and that the only Good and only Saviour might be recognized through the Son from age to age. And yet faith too, that one will receive, is a kind of prayer laid up gnostically within.

7.42. But if prayer becomes an occasion of converse with God, then no occasion of approach to God must be let slip. Indeed, when the holiness of the gnostic is interwoven with the blessed providence, through the voluntary confession it displays the perfect benefaction of God. For the holiness of the gnostic is, as it were, a kind of return upon providence, and a reciprocal goodwill on the part of the friend of God. For God is not good unwillingly, in the way that fire is hot; rather, the imparting of good things is voluntary with him, even if he anticipates the request. Nor again is the one who is saved saved unwillingly; for he is not without a soul, but, more than anything, will hasten toward salvation willingly and by deliberate choice. Therefore man received the commandments as having of himself an impulse toward whichever he might will of the things to be chosen and the things to be shunned. So then God does not do good by necessity, but does good by choice to those who turn of themselves. For the providence that comes to us from God is not a thing of servile ministry—as though proceeding from worse beings to better; but it is out of mercy toward our weakness that the nearer dispensations of providence are worked, just as is the case with the shepherds' care toward the sheep, and the king's toward his subjects, while we ourselves are obediently disposed toward our governors, those who orderly administer affairs according to the rank with which they were entrusted by God. They, then, are servants and ministers of the Divine who render the most free and most kingly service, that which is through devout judgement and knowledge.

7.43. Every place, then, is truly sacred in which we receive the conception of God, and every time. And when the man of good purpose, and grateful as well, asks through prayer, he in some way co-operates toward the receiving, gladly receiving what he longs for through the very things for which he prays. For when the Giver of good things receives our readiness, all the good things follow at once upon the very act of receiving. Indeed, through prayer the character is tested, how it is disposed toward what is fitting. And if voice and speech have been given us for the sake of understanding, how shall not God hear the soul itself and the mind—seeing that already soul perceives soul, and mind perceives mind? Whence God does not wait for the many-voiced tongues, as the interpreters among men do, but simply knows the thoughts of all; and what voice signifies to us, that our thought speaks to God, which thought, even before the creation, he knew would come into being. It is possible, then, not even to send forth one's prayer by voice, but only to strain all the spiritual part within toward the intelligible voice, in undistracted turning toward God. And since the dawn is an image of the day of birth, and from there the light increases, having first "shone forth out of darkness"—but also a day of the knowledge of the truth has risen, like the sun, upon those rolling about in ignorance—our prayers are toward the morning dawn. Whence too the most ancient of the shrines looked toward the west, that those standing face to face with the images might be taught to turn toward the east. "Let my prayer be set before you as incense," say the Psalms, "the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice."

7.44. For the wicked among men, then, prayer is most hurtful, not only to others, but to themselves as well. If, indeed, they should ask and obtain even the things they call good fortune, the obtaining harms them, since they are ignorant of how to use them. For they pray to acquire what they do not have, and ask for the seeming goods, not the real ones. But the gnostic asks for the continuance of the things he has acquired, for fitness for the things he is to pass over to, and for the eternity of the things he will not receive; and he prays that the truly good things, those concerning the soul, may both be his and abide. In this way he does not even reach out for anything that is absent, being content with what is present. For he is not wanting in his own proper goods, being already sufficient to himself out of the divine grace and knowledge. Rather, having become self-sufficient and in need of nothing besides, knowing the almighty will, and at once possessing and praying, having drawn near to the all-powerful Power, and having striven to be spiritual, through love without bound he has been united to the Spirit. This is the high-minded man, the one who possesses, in his knowledge, the most precious of all and the best of all things—keen in the application to contemplation, and possessing in his soul an abiding power over the things contemplated, that is, the penetrating sharpness of knowledge. And this power he strives as far as possible to acquire, having become master "of the things that war against the mind," and unceasingly attending upon contemplation, having trained himself by discipline both in the holding back from pleasures and in the right doing of things to be done. Besides these, having made use of much experience in learning and in life, he has frankness of speech—not that power of an unbarred tongue, simply so called, but a power that uses plain speech, hiding none of the things that may be said at the fitting season, where it is most needful, neither for favour nor for fear.

7.45. Having, then, grasped in a manner worthy of the subject the things concerning God, taught by the very truth in the mystic choir, he uses the word that exhorts toward the greatness of virtue—a word that displays virtue and what springs from it according to its worth—being made gnostically akin, with God-inspired uplifting of prayer, as far as may be, to things intelligible and spiritual. Whence he is ever gentle and mild, easy of access, easy to meet, patient of evil, fair-minded, of a good conscience, austere. This austerity of ours is directed not only toward incorruptibility, but toward freedom from temptation; for in no way does he show his soul yielding or capturable by pleasure and pain. He is a judge, if reason should call him to it, having become unbending, granting nothing whatever to the passions, walking unswervingly in the path where the just by nature proceeds—being well persuaded that all things are most nobly administered, and that the advance ever goes on toward the better for souls that have chosen virtue, until they come to the Good itself, having become, as it were, near to the great High Priest "at the doors" of the Father. This is, for us, the faithful gnostic, persuaded that the affairs of the world are administered in the best way. Indeed, he is well pleased with all that befalls.

7.46. With good reason, then, he seeks none of the things in life that are convenient for necessary use, persuaded that God, who knows all things, furnishes good things even to those who do not ask, whatever may be profitable. For just as, I think, to the artisan things are rendered after the manner of the artisan, and to the heathen after the heathen manner, so to the gnostic each thing is rendered after the gnostic manner. And the one converting from among the heathen will ask for faith; the one ascending into knowledge, for "the perfection of love." But the gnostic, already at the summit, prays that contemplation may increase and abide, just as the common man prays for continuous health. Yes, and he will ask never to fall away from virtue, co-operating especially that he may remain unfallen. For he knows that some even of the angels, having slipped through sloth, fell again to the ground, not yet having wrung themselves wholly out of their fitness for double-mindedness into that one settled disposition. But for the one who has been trained from here below into the height of knowledge and the lofty pre-eminence of the complete man, all things in time and place go before him on the road—for the one who has chosen and practises to live unwaveringly, through the everywhere-monotonous steadfastness of his judgement. But for those in whom there is still left over some heavy corner inclining downward, the part raised up by faith is dragged down. For the man who has, by gnostic discipline, made virtue a thing that cannot be cast away, the settled disposition becomes a second nature; and just as weight belongs to the stone, so to him knowledge becomes a thing that cannot be cast off—not unwillingly, but willingly, established by a rational and gnostic and provident power.

7.47. And since that which is not cast away through caution becomes, through good reasoning, a thing that cannot be cast away, he will hold fast to caution toward not sinning, and to good reasoning toward the irremovability of virtue. And knowledge seems to furnish good reasoning, teaching one to discern the things that can help toward the continuance of virtue. Greatest of all, then, is the knowledge of God. Therefore by it the irremovability of virtue is preserved. And he who has known God is holy and devout. The gnostic alone, then, has been shown by us to be devout. This man rejoices over the present goods, and exults over those promised, as already present. For they have not escaped him as though still absent, since through knowledge he has anticipated of what kind they are. Persuaded, then, by knowledge that each of the things to come is as it is, he possesses it. For that which is deficient and lacking is measured against what is fitting. If, then, he has acquired wisdom, and wisdom is divine, the one who partakes of that which needs nothing would himself be in need of nothing. For the imparting of wisdom does not come about by the activity and the partaker moving and holding back one another, nor by anything being taken away, nor by the giver becoming needy; rather, the activity is shown to be undiminished through the very imparting. So, then, the gnostic has all good things in respect of power, though not yet in respect of number—for otherwise he would be unchanging according to the God-inspired advances and dispensations that are due. With this man God too co-operates, having honoured him with a nearer oversight.

7.48. For have not all things come to be for the sake of good men, and for their use and benefit—nay rather, for their salvation? He would not, then, take away from these the things that are theirs for the sake of virtue—they on whose account the things that are have come to be. For it is plain that he would honour their good nature and their holy purpose, since he breathes strength even into those who have undertaken to live well, for the rest of their salvation—exhorting some only, but to those who have become worthy of themselves giving his aid as well. For everything is an added gift to the gnostic, if indeed his end is to know and to do each thing knowingly. And as the physician furnishes health to those who co-operate toward health, so too God furnishes eternal salvation to those who co-operate toward knowledge and right action; and, together with our doing—since the things that the commandments enjoin are in our power—the promise too is fulfilled. And this, it seems to me, is also nobly said among the Greeks: a certain athlete, no mean man, in the days of old, having for a long time trained his poor body well toward manliness, went up to Olympia, and, looking toward the statue of Pisaean Zeus, said: "If, O Zeus, all things have been duly prepared by me for the contest, come, give me the victory in justice." For so it is with the gnostic too: when he has irreproachably and with a good conscience fulfilled all that lies in his own power, toward learning and toward training and toward well-doing and toward being well-pleasing to God, then the whole is brought together for his most perfect salvation. These things, then, are required of us: of the things in our power and of the things that pertain to us, both present and absent—choice and longing and acquisition and use and continuance.

7.49. Therefore he who holds converse with God must have his soul undefiled and sincerely unstained—most of all, having wrought himself wholly good; or, if not, at least making progress toward knowledge and reaching out for it, but utterly drawn away from the works of vice. And it is fitting, too, that all prayers be made fairly, and in company with the fair; for it is perilous to be set down as a sharer in the sins of others. Concerning these things, then, the gnostic will pray together with those who have believed in the more common way, and concerning whom it befits him also to act together with them. And his whole life is a holy festival. His sacrifices, accordingly, are prayers and praises, and the readings from the Scriptures before the meal, and psalms and hymns during the meal and before sleep, and again prayers by night. Through these he unites himself to "the divine choir," set, out of the continual remembrance, into ever-mindful contemplation. What then? Does he not know also that other sacrifice—the giving, according to those in need, both of doctrines and of money? Yes indeed. But the prayer through the mouth he does not make with many words, having learned from the Lord what one ought to ask. In every place, then—yet not openly or visibly before the many—he will pray; while walking, in converse, in quietness, in reading, and in his works that are according to reason, he prays in every way. And even if in the very "storehouse" of the soul he is but thinking, and "with unspeakable groanings calls upon the Father," he who is near is present even while the man still speaks. And since there are three ends of every action, he works all things for the noble and the profitable; but the doing of a thing for the sake of pleasure he leaves to those who pursue the common life.

8.50. Far indeed should it be that the one examined in such piety should be ready either to lie or to swear an oath. For an oath is a determining acknowledgement with the additional taking-on of the divine. But the one who is once faithful—how could he show himself faithless, so as even to need an oath, and not rather make his very life a firm and fixed oath? He lives and conducts himself, and shows the trustworthiness of his confession in a life and a word that do not waver and are steadfast. And if doing wrong lies in the judgement of the one who acts and speaks, and not in the suffering of the one wronged, he will neither lie nor swear falsely, as one wronging the Divine, knowing that it is by nature unharmable; but neither, for his neighbour's sake, will he lie or transgress anything—him whom he has learned to love, even if he happen to be no acquaintance; and for his own sake, all the more, he will neither lie nor swear falsely, since he would never willingly be found unjust toward himself. But neither will he swear, having chosen to set, in assent, only the "yes," and in denial the "no," as his adverb. For to swear is to bring forward an oath, or to bring something forward, as it were, by way of an oath, affirmatively from the intention.

8.51. It suffices him, then, to add to his assent or his denial the words "I speak truly," for the setting-forth of his answer's firmness to those who do not discern it. For one ought, I think, to have toward outsiders a life worthy of trust, so that one is not even asked for an oath; and toward oneself and toward those who understand, fair-mindedness, which is voluntary righteousness. Accordingly, the gnostic keeps his oath well, yet is not prone to swearing, coming to swear but rarely, and even then in the manner we have described. And yet the speaking of truth under oath comes about with the accord of what is according to truth; the keeping of an oath, then, results according to the right doing of one's duties. Where, then, is there any further need of an oath for the man who lives at the height of truth? For the one who does not even swear is far indeed from swearing falsely; and the one who transgresses none of the things agreed upon would never even swear at all, seeing that the ratification both of transgression and of fulfilment lies in deeds—just as, indeed, lying and false swearing lie in speaking and in swearing contrary to duty. But the one who lives justly, transgressing none of his duties, where the judgement of truth is examined, keeps his oath in his deeds; superfluous, then, for him is the witness of the tongue. Persuaded, then, that God is everywhere always, and ashamed not to speak the truth, and knowing that lying is unworthy of himself, he is content with the divine conscience and his own alone; and in this way he neither lies nor does anything contrary to the agreements, and in this way too he neither swears an oath when required, nor ever denies—lest he lie—even though he should die under torture.

9.52. But the gnostic dignity is heightened still further and more in the one who has taken up the presidency of teaching others, undertaking in word and deed the dispensation of the greatest good upon earth, through which he mediates conjunction and fellowship toward the Divine. And as those who do service to earthly things pray to the images as though they heard, making their firm agreements upon them, so, in the case of the living images—men—the true magnificence of the Word is received from the trustworthy teacher, and the benefit done to these is referred to the Lord himself, after whose image the man who is truly a man, in teaching, fashions and transforms anew unto salvation the man being catechized. For as the Greeks call iron "Ares" and wine "Dionysus," by a certain reference, so the gnostic, reckoning the benefit of his neighbours to be his own salvation, would reasonably be called a living image of the Lord—not in respect of the property of form, but in respect of the symbol of power and the likeness of his preaching.

9.53. Whatever, then, he has in mind, this he also carries upon the tongue toward those worthy to hear, out of assent, speaking from judgement and at the same time living it. For he both thinks true things and speaks the truth—except when, perchance, by way of treatment, like a physician toward the sick for the salvation of the suffering, he will lie, or speak a falsehood, as the sophists put it. Thus the noble Apostle circumcised Timothy, though he cried aloud and wrote that circumcision made with hands profits nothing; but lest, by tearing them all at once away from the Law toward the circumcision of the heart that is of faith, he should compel the Hebrew hearers, who were still unbridled, to break away from the synagogue—accommodating himself to the Jews, he "became a Jew, that he might gain all." He, then, who descends only as far as accommodation, for the sake of his neighbours' salvation—the bare accommodation for the salvation of those for whose sake he accommodates himself—partaking of no hypocrisy, because of the danger that hangs over the just from the jealous, this man is in no way compelled; but only for the benefit of his neighbours will he do certain things which he would not otherwise have done for their own sake, were he not doing them on their account. This man gives himself for the Church, for the friends whom he himself "begot" in faith, as an example to those able to take up the supreme dispensation of the man-loving and God-loving teacher—for the establishment of the truth of his words, for the operation of his love toward the Lord. He is unenslaved by fear, true in word, patient in toil, unwilling ever to lie even in the spoken word, and in this too always achieving sinlessness. For the lie itself, being spoken with a certain deceit, is no idle word, but works toward evil.

9.54. On every side, then, the gnostic alone bears witness to the truth, both in deed and in word; for he always does rightly in all things absolutely—in word and in act and in the very thought. This, then, to speak as in a running survey, is the godliness of the Christian. If indeed he does these things fittingly and according to right reason, he does them devoutly and justly. And if these things are so, the gnostic alone would be in truth devout and just and godly. The Christian, then, is not an atheist—for this was what was proposed to be shown to the philosophers—so that he will in no way ever do anything evil or shameful, which is unjust. Accordingly, neither is he impious, but he alone is in truth godly, holily and fittingly approaching, according to the true godliness, the God who truly is—the all-ruling and all-kingly and almighty—holily turning toward him.

10.55. For knowledge is, so to speak, a kind of perfecting of man as man, completed through the science of things divine, in character and in life and in word—in accord and agreement with itself and with the divine Word. For through it faith is perfected, the believer becoming perfect in this way alone. Faith, then, is a kind of inward good, which, even without seeking God, confesses that he is and glorifies him as existing. Whence one must, being led up from this faith and increased in it by the grace of God, attain the knowledge concerning him, as far as may be. And we say that knowledge differs from the wisdom which comes into being through teaching: for wherever there is any knowledge, there is also, by all means, wisdom; but wherever there is any wisdom, there is not by all means knowledge—for it is only in the matter of the spoken word that the name of wisdom appears. Nevertheless, not to doubt concerning God, but to believe, is the foundation of knowledge; and both are Christ—both the foundation and the building upon it, through whom are both the beginning and the ends. And the extremes are not taught—the beginning and the end, I mean faith and love; but knowledge, handed down by tradition according to the grace of God to those who show themselves worthy of the teaching, is entrusted like a deposit, from which the worth of love shines forth, from light to light. For it is said, "to him who has it shall be added"—to faith, knowledge; to knowledge, love; and to love, the inheritance.

10.56. And this comes about whenever a man is hung upon the Lord through faith and through knowledge and through love, and ascends together with him to where the God and Guardian of our faith and love is. Whence at the end knowledge is handed down to those fit for it and approved—because there is need of more preparation and previous training, both toward the hearing of the things spoken, and toward the composure of life, and toward having advanced, by intensity, beyond the righteousness that is according to the Law. This knowledge leads us to the endless and perfect end, teaching us beforehand the manner of life we shall have, according to God, with gods, once we have been freed from all chastisement and punishment—which we endure, because of our sins, for our saving instruction. After this redemption the reward and the honours are rendered to those made perfect, when they have ceased from purification and ceased from all other ministry, even if it be holy and among holy ones.
