Both in substance, then, and in conception, and in beginning, and in pre-eminence, we say that the ancient and Catholic Church is alone—gathering, "into the unity of one faith," that which is according to the proper covenants, or rather according to the one covenant in different times, by the will of one God through one Lord, those already ordained—whom God foreordained, having known before the foundation of the world that they would be just. But also the pre-eminence of the Church, just as the beginning of its constitution, is according to the Monad, surpassing all other things and having nothing like or equal to itself.

17.108. These things, then, also for later. But of the heresies, some are named from a name, like that from Valentinus and Marcion and Basilides—even though they boast of bringing forward the opinion of Matthias; for the teaching of all the apostles was one, just as the tradition was also one. Others are named from a place, like the Peratici; others from a nation, like that of the Phrygians; others from an activity, like that of the Encratites; others from peculiar doctrines, like that of the Docetae and that of the Haematites; others from suppositions and from the men they have honoured, like the Cainists and those called Ophites; and others from the lawless things they practised and dared, like those of the Simonians who are called Entychites.

18.109. Having, then, pointed out a small opening "to those who love the contemplation of the truth," from the law concerning sacrifices, regarding both the common Jews and the heresies—as unclean, being mystically distinguished from the divine Church, by the law of clean and unclean animals—let us bring the discourse to a close. For the Scripture hands down as clean and acceptable to God those of the sacrificial animals that part the hoof and chew the cud, as figuring that the just make their journey toward the Father and toward the Son through faith (for this is the steadfastness of the cleft-footed)—those who "meditate on the oracles of God night and day," and ruminate them in the receptacle of the soul that holds learning. Which gnostic exercise the law allegorizes as the cud-chewing of the clean animal. But those that have neither of these, or one without the other, it sets apart as unclean. Accordingly, the things that chew the cud but do not part the hoof hint at the many Jews, who have the oracles of God upon their lips, but do not have faith, and the foundation that conveys, through the Son, to the Father, leaning upon the truth. Whence the race of such cattle is also slippery, as not being cloven-footed nor leaning upon the double support of faith. "For no one," it is said, "knows the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son shall reveal him." And, again, unclean in like manner are those that part the hoof but do not chew the cud. For these signify the heretics, who have set foot upon the name of Father and Son, but are too weak to work fine and to grind smooth the exact clearness of the oracles, and besides who pursue the works of righteousness more grossly, not more exactly—if indeed they pursue them at all.

18.110. To certain such the Lord says: "Why do you call me 'Lord, Lord,' and do not the things I say?" And altogether unclean are those that neither part the hoof nor chew the cud. "But you, O Megarians," says Theognis, "are neither third nor fourth nor twelfth, neither in account nor in number," but rather "like the chaff which the wind drives away from the face of the earth," and "like a drop from a bucket." Now that these things have been brought to an end for us, and the ethical division has been sketched as in summary, having sown in here and there—scattered and dispersed, as we promised—the live coals of the doctrines of true knowledge, so that it may not be easy for the chance uninitiated reader to find out the holy traditions, let us pass on to our promise.

18.111. The Miscellanies are somewhat like, not those parks set in order with trees planted in rows for the pleasure of the eye, but rather like some shady and thick-grown hill planted with cypresses and plane-trees, with laurel and ivy, and at the same time with apple-trees and olives and figs—the planting deliberately mingled of fruit-bearing and unfruitful trees together, on account of those who dare to filch and steal the ripe fruit; the writing willing to lie hid. From which the husbandman, transplanting and re-grafting, will set in order a fair park and a delightful grove. The Miscellanies, then, aim neither at arrangement nor at style, since indeed on purpose both the diction is not such as the Greeks would have it, and the sowing-in of the doctrines has been made secretly and not according to the plain truth—preparing the readers, if any chance to be such, to be lovers of toil and discoverers. For many and various are the baits, by reason of the differences among the fish. And now, after this seventh Book of our Miscellanies, we shall make the discourse of what follows from another beginning.
